bodyText: She walks now, or she's working on it. The first few weeks of walking look uncertain — wide stance, arms out, a lot of sitting back down. She's not failing at walking. She's learning it. Leave room for her to fall and get back up.

He points at things to show you what he's interested in, and he looks back at you to see if you're looking too. He wants to share what he's seeing. That desire to share experience is one of the most human things there is. Follow his point and say the name of whatever he's pointing at.

She may have six to eight words now. They may not sound like the real words — 'ba' for ball, 'nana' for banana — but if she uses them consistently to mean the same thing, they count. The vocabulary will grow faster than you expect over the next few months.

He copies everything. You sweep and he finds something to sweep with. You talk on the phone and he picks up a toy phone. You put on shoes and he tries to put his on. He's doing his job, which is learning how the world works by watching you.

Tantrums are starting or will start soon. They happen because she has feelings that are larger than her ability to manage them or express them. The tantrum is not a strategy — it's an overflow. Staying calm when she isn't is the whole job.
He eats with a spoon now, or he's learning to. It takes time and makes a mess. Let him do it himself even when it would be faster to feed him. The practice matters more than the efficiency.

She has a few words but understands far more than she can say. Her receptive vocabulary — what she understands when she hears it — is much larger than her expressive vocabulary. She knows more than she can tell you.

Bedtime is when most toddlers test limits, because they don't want to stop. A consistent routine — bath, book, same song, same sequence — is the most effective tool there is. Not because it forces sleep, but because it signals that sleep is coming.

He's a climber now or he's about to be. He'll climb onto furniture, out of furniture, up stairs, and into whatever he can reach. The answer is not to stop him from climbing — it's to give him safe things to climb and stay close when the thing isn't safe.

She points to pictures in books when you name them. She looks at the dog and you say 'dog' and she points to the right picture. She's connecting words to images to concepts. Read with her every day even if it's only for ten minutes.

He says 'no' very clearly now, in multiple ways. He shakes his head. He says the word. He pushes things away. He turns his face. He has learned to refuse, which is a developmental milestone and also, sometimes, very tiring to live with.

She drinks from a cup now, more or less. There are still spills and there will be for a while. The cup is the right direction regardless. The bottle will phase out on its own if you stop offering it routinely.

Fifteen months. He walks, he talks in his own way, he has opinions, he has preferences, he has people he loves. He has become a person with a personality that is recognizably his. You've been watching this happen for over a year.

She walks well now — not steadily, not gracefully, but with confidence and speed. She can run, sort of. She can go up stairs if she has something to hold. The body she has at eighteen months is a completely different instrument than the one she had at twelve.

He has ten or more words now, or he's working toward it. They may not be clear to anyone outside your household. That's fine. You're his primary audience, and you understand him. Strangers will catch up.
She shows you things — brings you a toy to show you, holds up a picture in a book, points to something interesting on a walk. She's inviting you into her world. Go.

He pretends. He feeds a stuffed animal. He puts a doll to bed. He stirs an empty pot. That pretend play is not just fun — it's how he's practicing the logic of the world, and it's an early sign of the imagination that will be with him for the rest of his life.

She may have a tantrum when you leave her at daycare or with a caregiver. That distress is not evidence that something is wrong with the care arrangement. It's evidence that she's attached to you, which is the right outcome. She settles. You'll find out she settles.

He pushes toys while walking. He stacks blocks and knocks them down. He puts things in containers and dumps them out. These are not games — they're experiments in physics and spatial reasoning. He's learning something from each of them.
She points to body parts when you name them — nose, eyes, ears, tummy. She's building a map of her own body. Point to yours and say the word. Point to hers. She'll start doing it back.

He's starting to do simple household tasks alongside you — carrying something to the trash, putting his shoes by the door, wiping the table with a cloth. He wants to help. Let him. The help is usually more symbolic than practical. That's fine.

Sleep may get harder before it gets easier. The 18-month sleep regression is real — it often coincides with developmental leaps in language and cognition that disrupt sleep. If things were going well and then stopped, that's probably why.

She shakes her head to mean no now, sometimes without saying the word. She nods to mean yes. She waves goodbye. She claps when pleased. She's become fluent in a whole language of gesture that she invented alongside the words.

He may be screened for autism at the eighteen-month well visit. This is routine — it happens for every child. If the screen leads to a follow-up, that follow-up is worth doing. Early is better for everything that benefits from support.

She's starting to understand the concept of 'mine.' She'll say it or sign it or make it very clear. That possessiveness is the beginning of a sense of self — of understanding that she is a separate person with things that belong to her. It will get more annoying before it gets more sophisticated.

Eighteen months. He's a toddler in full now — mobile, verbal in his own way, emotional, curious, independent to the degree his coordination allows. The newborn year is fully behind you. What's ahead is different and harder in some ways and better in others.

The language explosion is here or coming. Some children add several words a week at this age. Others add them more slowly. The range is wide. What matters more than word count is whether she's communicating — pointing, gesturing, making meaningful sounds. Talk to your pediatrician at the two-year visit with anything on your mind.

He says two-word combinations now — 'more milk,' 'daddy go,' 'big dog.' Two words together is a real milestone in expressive language. It shows he's understanding that words can be combined to mean things that neither word means alone.
She runs now, and she falls less than she did. She climbs with intention. She can kick a ball. Her physical world has expanded enormously in the past six months, and so has her confidence in it.

He plays alongside other children rather than with them. He's aware of them, interested in them, but he's not collaborating yet. That's normal — cooperative play comes later. Parallel play is the stage before it.

She has opinions about what she wears, what she eats, what she does next, and who holds her. These opinions will multiply and intensify over the next year. This is not defiance — it's autonomy developing. There's a difference.

He scribbles now. Give him crayons and paper and let him go. The scribbling is his hand learning to make marks on purpose. He can't draw anything recognizable yet, but he knows he made something, and he's proud of it. Put it on the refrigerator.

She remembers things now — she'll go back to where she left a toy, she'll remember what happened earlier in the day, she'll ask for something she had yesterday. Her memory is extending backward in a way it didn't before.

Tantrums peak somewhere in the second year. They're not a phase that passes all at once — they taper. What speeds the tapering is language: the more words he has to express what he wants, the less his body has to do the expressing. Keep narrating. Keep naming emotions.
She sorts shapes and colors now — not perfectly, but with intention. She knows that some things go together and others don't. She's building the categories that thinking is built from.

He follows two-step instructions. 'Pick up the ball and put it in the box.' That sounds simple. It requires holding two steps in working memory simultaneously while executing them in order. Six months ago that wasn't possible.

She plays make-believe with real feeling now — her dolls have emotions, her stuffed animals have needs, her pretend cooking is serious business. She's practicing empathy, narrative, and cause and effect all at once.

He's starting to understand what he does affects how other people feel. He'll look at your face after he does something, checking your expression. He's learning the beginning of empathy by reading you.
She completes familiar sentences in books — you start the line and she says the last word. She knows these books by heart. That's memory, language, and the pleasure of a known thing all at once.
He uses 'me' and 'you' now, getting them right more than he gets them wrong. Pronouns are complicated — they change depending on who's speaking. That he's sorted this out at all is impressive.

Two years old. The birthday is worth marking, even if she doesn't know what a birthday is yet. She is a person who walks, runs, talks in her own way, has friends she cares about, and loves you specifically. That happened in two years.
He walks up and down stairs now, one foot at a time, holding on. Stairs are still something to watch. But he's not afraid of them anymore. He's decided they're navigable, and he's right.

She says sentences with two to four words. Those sentences are sometimes about what's happening right now, and sometimes about something that already happened. The past tense is arriving. That's a significant cognitive step.

He plays chase, he plays hide-and-seek in his own version, he plays games that have rules he invented. The rules matter to him even when they change. That's the beginning of understanding that games have structure.

She may have a best friend now — a child she asks for by name, whose presence makes the day better. Friendships at two are not what they'll be at seven, but the emotional investment is real. Don't dismiss it.

He builds towers of four blocks or more. He knows what he's doing — he's testing how high he can go before it falls. He'll figure out what makes a tower stable before he has any words for the physics involved.
She knows names and faces and places and routines. She has a map of her world that's more detailed than you realize. Take her somewhere new and watch how carefully she takes it all in.

He gets excited in a particular way before things he loves — the park, a certain person, a certain food. That anticipatory joy is a sign of memory and expectation working together. He knows what's coming, and he's happy about it.

She asks 'why.' It starts now and continues for several years. The 'why' is not always a request for information — sometimes it's a way of extending the conversation, of staying in contact with you. Answer as genuinely as you can.
He names a friend. He talks about her at home, asks for her, notices when she isn't there. His social world is extending beyond family in a new way.

She dresses herself, partially. She can put on some things without help and needs help with others. Let her do the parts she can. It takes longer. That's the price of independence, and it's worth paying.
Two years and a few months. He is comprehensively himself now — the personality that was visible at six months has not changed direction, just deepened. You know who he is. You've known for a while.

Three is when the world opens up. She talks in full sentences now, she plays with other children rather than just alongside them, she has a sense of herself as a person separate from you. That separateness is something you helped build. It's the right outcome.

He can name most familiar things. He knows his own name, his age, whether he's a boy or a girl. He knows the names of his friends. He knows the names of things in his world with a completeness that wasn't there six months ago.

She separates from you more easily now. The drop-off at preschool that was anguish at two is sometimes barely a goodbye at three. She knows you come back. She trusts that now in a way she had to learn.

He shows concern for a friend who is crying. He'll go to them, or look worried, or tell you about it afterward. That concern is the beginning of real empathy — not just reading emotion, but feeling something in response to it.

She follows three-step instructions now. 'Go to your room, get your shoes, and bring them here.' That's three things held in order in working memory, which is more than most three-year-olds could do six months ago.

He understands 'mine' and 'his' and 'hers.' He's starting to understand that other people have feelings about things that are theirs. The concept of property and the feelings around it are getting more sophisticated.

She runs easily, climbs well, pedals a tricycle. Her body does things she couldn't imagine at eighteen months. Physical confidence at three is worth noticing — it carries over into social confidence in ways that aren't always obvious.

He has friends he cares about. He talks about them. He wants to see them. He notices when they're not there. These friendships are not casual — they matter to him in a way that's worth taking seriously.

She dresses and undresses herself now, more or less. There are still inside-out shirts and backward pants and shoes on the wrong feet. Let her do it anyway. The practice is more important than the result.
He draws people — a circle with some lines for limbs. That's not just art. It's him encoding his understanding of what a person is. His drawings will get more detailed as his understanding does.

She may have real fears now — the dark, dogs, loud noises, something specific to her. Don't tell her the fear isn't real. It is real to her. Stay close. Name the fear. Gradually, with time and your presence, most fears at three don't last.

He tells stories. They may not make sense to you — they're not sequential, they jump around, they mix real and invented. That doesn't matter. He's practicing narrative, which is how humans organize experience. Let him tell you.

She uses 'I' and 'me' and 'you' correctly now, most of the time. Those pronouns were confusing for months. The fact that they're settled is a sign of how much her understanding of self and other has developed.

He plays make-believe with rules and roles — he's the doctor, you're the patient, and the rules must be followed. The role-playing is practice for the social world: there are parts, there are expectations, there is a script that changes when you change it.

She knows what's real and what's make-believe most of the time. The line is still blurry — Santa Claus, monsters, what happened in a dream — but she's working it out. Don't worry about the blurriness. It resolves.

He copies you in ways that are sometimes flattering and sometimes not. He uses your phrases. He adopts your mannerisms. He tells people things you said in ways that reveal exactly how much he's listening. He is always listening.

She has conversations now — real ones, with back-and-forth and new information and responses to what you say. Those conversations are one of the better things about the three-year-old years. Make time for them.
He understands time in a loose way — yesterday, today, tomorrow, later, soon. He can't tell time yet, but the concept that time has sequence is there. That sequence is the beginning of planning.

She counts to ten, possibly beyond. She doesn't fully understand what the numbers mean yet — she's counting as a sequence, not as a quantity. The conceptual understanding of number comes gradually throughout the preschool years.

He has a best friend, or something close to it — a child he talks about at home, wants to see, misses when apart. That friendship is real. It may not last to adulthood but it matters now, and what he learns from it matters.

She needs structure, even when she pushes against it. The routines and rules aren't constraints — they're the container that makes her feel safe enough to test limits. The testing is healthy. The container is what makes it safe.

He shows affection spontaneously now — comes to hug you for no reason, holds your hand without being asked, tells you he loves you in his own way. That affection is genuine. It's the relationship you built.

She may start asking big questions — where do babies come from, what happens when you die, why is the sky blue. Answer them honestly at the level she can understand. She can handle more truth than you might think.

He's going to preschool or he will soon. The transition is easier if he's visited, if he knows someone there, if the drop-off routine is consistent. He may have hard days even after weeks of good ones. That's not regression. That's Tuesday.

She has an imagination now that is genuinely its own thing — she invents characters, gives them names, makes up stories that have beginnings and middles and her version of an ending. That imagination is a gift. Take it seriously.

Three years old. He is, in every meaningful sense, a person — one with a history you both share, with preferences and relationships and a sense of himself in the world. You built this alongside him, one year at a time.

Four is when children become genuinely creative — not just imitating, but inventing. She makes up games with rules she designed, tells stories with plots she constructed, draws things that exist only in her mind. That creativity is worth protecting. Don't fill all the unstructured time.
He prefers other children to being alone now. He has social needs that he knows how to pursue. A playdate is not optional enrichment — it's nourishment for him at this stage.

She knows the difference between what's real and what's make-believe most of the time — but the line is still moveable in interesting ways. She knows her stuffed animals aren't really alive. She still talks to them. Both things are true at once. That's fine.

He asks 'why' constantly now. The best answers are honest ones. If you don't know, say you don't know and find out together. He will remember that you took his questions seriously, long after he's forgotten the answers.

She cooperates with other children in sustained ways now — building something together, playing a game that requires real turn-taking. That cooperation is new. It means she can hold her own intentions alongside another person's and negotiate between them.

He tells stories with beginnings, middles, and ends. He may not always get them in the right order, but the structure is there. Narrative structure at four is a cognitive achievement, not just a social one.
She hops on one foot. She catches a bounced ball most of the time. She can use scissors with supervision. Her fine and gross motor skills have been building steadily for four years, and it shows.
He knows some letters and possibly some numbers. He can write his name, or most of it. He can print some letters. He's at the edge of literacy — not there yet, but he can see it from here.
She understands time in a more sophisticated way now — morning and afternoon and night, yesterday and today and tomorrow. She can look forward to something with more patience than she could at three.

He helps with simple chores without being asked, sometimes. He carries his plate to the sink. He picks up his toys when reminded. He's learning that he's part of a household that requires his contribution. That feeling of being needed matters.

She has a theory of other minds now — she understands that other people have thoughts and feelings and perspectives that are different from hers. This is called theory of mind, and it's the cognitive foundation of empathy. It arrives fully somewhere between three and five.
He may have a best friend he talks about with real feeling — someone who matters to him in a way that's clearly more than casual. Let that friendship be important. It is important.

She can get dressed by herself now. She picks her own clothes when you let her. The choices are sometimes creative. Let her wear the thing. Getting dressed is an arena where she can have complete autonomy, and the stakes are low.

He's starting to understand that reading is possible — that those marks on the page mean something specific, that he could learn to read them. He may not be reading yet, but the concept is there. Surround him with books. Read to him every day.
She knows her full name and possibly her address and phone number. She knows these things because you said them enough times that they became part of her. Keep saying them.

He plays games with rules that came from somewhere else — not rules he invented, but rules that exist in the world. Board games, card games, made-up games on the playground with complex protocols. He follows the rules, mostly, and gets upset when others don't.

She draws a person with at least four body parts. Those drawings are self-portraits, more or less — how she understands what a person looks like. Keep them. The drawings will change and the earlier ones will tell you something you'll want to remember.

He sings songs all the way through. He has favorite songs that he requests, that he changes the words to, that he performs at unexpected moments. Music is one of the earliest forms of memory and he's using it.

She's ready for more independence than you may feel comfortable giving. She can play alone for twenty minutes, go to the neighbor's yard, walk to the corner of the block. The appropriate amount of independence at four is more than it was at three. Adjust gradually.

He's going to kindergarten next year, or close to it. He's ready in ways that you may not fully see yet. He can listen. He can sit still for a while. He can follow instructions. He has something to say and ways to say it.

She may seem, at four, like she has a clear personality that isn't going to change. She's right. The person she is at four is a reliable preview of the person she'll be at fourteen and forty. You already know who she is.

He asks big questions now — what happens when we die, why is the world the way it is, where did we come from. He can handle honest answers at his level. He's already thinking about things that matter.

She has fears that are specific and sometimes surprising. Those fears deserve to be taken seriously even when they seem irrational. At four, what matters is not whether the fear makes sense, but that she has someone who takes it seriously while she works it out.

He's four years old, which means you've been doing this for four years. The first year was all survival. The second was all walking and talking. The third was all feelings. The fourth is when the person shows up completely. That person is remarkable.

She's going to start school soon. Whatever she needs to know for kindergarten, she mostly already knows. What she needs more than anything else is to know that she's loved, that she's capable, and that you'll be there when it's done. She knows all of that.

Four years old. He walks into rooms with confidence. He has friends. He has a personality. He has things to say about the world. He knows you love him. That's everything that was supposed to happen, and it did.

Five is kindergarten. It is the first time the world asks something specific of her, and she is ready for it in ways that surprise parents every year. She can sit still. She can listen. She has things to say. She will be fine, even on the days she isn't.

He wants to please his friends now in a way that matters to him. What other children think is starting to count. That's the beginning of something long and complicated — the social world he'll navigate for the rest of his life. The foundation you built at home is what he'll carry into it.

She can tell you a simple story with a beginning, middle, and end. She uses full sentences. She can be understood by strangers. She talks about what she likes and what she's interested in. She has a voice and she uses it.

He knows what's real and what's make-believe, clearly, most of the time. The imaginary world doesn't disappear — it becomes more deliberate. He chooses to enter it now instead of living in it. That's a shift.

She counts to twenty, or beyond. She understands that numbers represent quantity. She's at the beginning of mathematical thinking, which is really just the beginning of understanding pattern and structure. It starts with counting.

He's learning to read, or he's on the edge of it. He recognizes letters and many letter sounds. He may be sounding out simple words. Reading is one of the few skills that, once you have it, you can't imagine not having. He's almost there.

She hops, she skips, she can stand on one foot for ten seconds. She can do a somersault. She swings herself on a swing. Her body is capable in ways that she takes for granted, because it's been building capability for five years.

He talks about what happens at school. He has opinions about his teacher, his friends, his lunch. Ask questions that can't be answered with yes or no — not 'did you have a good day' but 'what was the most interesting thing that happened.' He has things to tell you.
She has her own sense of humor now — things she finds funny that you might not have predicted, jokes she makes, wordplay she discovers. That humor is hers. It will be hers for the rest of her life.

He knows his address and phone number and full name. He knows how to get help if he needs it. He understands the difference between safe adults and others. He's becoming someone who can navigate the world without you at his side every moment. That was always the goal.

She has friends who are real to her — people she loves, who she misses, whose opinions she cares about. Her social world is genuinely her own now. It belongs to her in a way that your social world doesn't.

Five years old. He was born five years ago, and everything that happened since then was the work. The conversations, the nights, the hard months, the good seasons, the learning and the being there. You did it. So did he.

Patricia has something to say before we end. You came here at the beginning, when you didn't know what you were doing. Most people don't, at the beginning. You learned as you went, which is the only way there is.

The child you have now — the one who walks into school on their own and has opinions and friends and a life that is increasingly theirs — is the child you raised. That's a different sentence than it sounds like. You didn't just keep them alive. You helped them become.

There were days when you did it badly, or when the circumstances made it nearly impossible, or when you looked at them and felt something other than what you thought you should feel. That's all true, and it doesn't change what you built.

You can still call on me when you need to. There's always more — the school years, the adolescent years, the years of letting go. Patricia will be here. But this is the end of what the app was designed for. The early years. The years before school, when everything was new and the nights were long and you needed someone who had been here before.
I've been here before. I've watched a lot of families do what you just did. Most of them thought they were doing it wrong more often than they were. Most of them were doing it right.
Take care of yourselves. — Patricia
